---
title: "documentation, fairness & approvals"
---

## define the decision and its owner

- governance assigns responsibility, review processes, and evidence requirements across the ml lifecycle
- intended use states the task, users, population, and setting a model was evaluated for; out-of-scope use states where that evidence does not support use
- an owner maintains the system and responds to issues; a reviewer checks evidence before a consequential change
- the nist ai risk management framework organises risk work into govern, map, measure, and manage [framework overview](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework)

## write a model card

- a model card documents a model’s purpose, data, evaluation, limitations, and ethical considerations [model cards paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.03993)
- keep it with the versioned model and evaluation report; update it when data, intended use, or behaviour changes
- this yaml template starts a record for the synthetic classifier used in these notes

```yaml
model_id: synthetic-classifier-v1
owner: learning-demo-maintainer
intended_use: synthetic binary classification exercise
out_of_scope: patient care or real-world decisions
data_version: replace-with-dataset-fingerprint
code_version: replace-with-git-commit
evaluation_report: reports/evaluation.json
limitations:
  - synthetic data cannot establish real-world performance
  - subgroup estimates need adequate labelled samples
review_status: pending
```

- replace example identifiers with the exact artifact, data, and code versions; attach sample sizes, metrics, uncertainty, and failure cases

## check performance across groups

- subgroup evaluation measures results separately for relevant populations or settings, such as age bands, sites, or scanner types
- selection rate is the fraction predicted positive; true positive rate is the fraction of actual positives detected; false positive rate is the fraction of actual negatives incorrectly flagged
- demographic parity compares selection rates; equalized odds compares both true and false positive rates across groups [fairness metric definitions](https://fairlearn.org/main/user_guide/assessment/common_fairness_metrics.html)
- metrics capture different questions and can conflict; choose them around the decision and its potential harms rather than treating one score as proof of fairness
- this tiny synthetic example uses pandas for tabular analysis and scikit-learn for a binary confusion matrix

```python
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix

data = pd.DataFrame({
    "group": ["a"] * 4 + ["b"] * 4,
    "target": [0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1],
    "score": [0.1, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.9],
})
threshold = 0.5
rows = []
for group, part in data.groupby("group"):
    predicted = (part["score"] >= threshold).astype(int)
    tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(
        part["target"], predicted, labels=[0, 1]
    ).ravel()
    rows.append({
        "group": group, "n": len(part),
        "positives": int(tp + fn), "negatives": int(tn + fp),
        "selection_rate": float(predicted.mean()),
        "true_positive_rate": tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else None,
        "false_positive_rate": fp / (tn + fp) if tn + fp else None,
    })
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))
```

- group a has true positive rate 1 and false positive rate 0.5; group b has true positive rate 0.5 and false positive rate 0
- four rows per group demonstrate the calculation, not reliable population estimates; undefined rates stay missing when a denominator is zero
- keep the threshold fixed for comparison, assess label quality and coverage, and report uncertainty and intersecting groups where sample sizes allow
- fairlearn is a fairness assessment toolkit; its `MetricFrame` computes overall and subgroup metrics and supports bootstrap intervals [metricframe reference](https://fairlearn.org/main/api_reference/generated/fairlearn.metrics.MetricFrame.html)

## review, release, and retain evidence

- an approval gate blocks promotion until an authorized reviewer accepts the required evidence; passing automated metrics alone does not provide that approval
- attach the frozen artifact id, evaluation and subgroup reports, known limitations, monitoring plan, and rollback target to the decision
- github environments can require deployment reviewers; configure the environment’s protection rules as well as referencing it in the deployment job, subject to repository and plan support [deployment reviews](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/deploy/configure-and-manage-deployments/review-deployments)
- an audit trail records who acted, what changed, when, and why; keep authenticated reviewer identities and protect records from unauthorized changes
- a local yaml field such as `review_status: approved` is documentation, not an enforced approval gate
- after release, review [monitoring signals](../monitoring/monitoring.qmd), revisit limitations, and investigate incidents with a named owner and recorded corrective actions
